16:I[12454,["/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/08cykig6vtx_p.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/07qi2okp-.yp9.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0frujd.eyhz4o.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0n4z.7yu76je-.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0otjhi71vbmnx.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/0j1uy9t~zxcf0.js","/paper-daily-site/_next/static/chunks/1304s0wcp2kce.js"],"WeeklyView"]
17:T893,FROST has two main ingredients: real-anchored utility estimation and conditional filtering.

For utility estimation, each training step draws both a real batch and a synthetic batch. The method maintains an exponential moving average of gradients from recent real batches, which serves as a smoothed reference direction for the real-data objective. Each synthetic sample is then scored by the alignment between its gradient and this real-gradient reference. The intuition is straightforward: if a synthetic sample pushes parameters in a direction similar to what recent real data prefers, it is more likely to be useful; if it points away, it is more likely to be harmful or off-distribution.

The second ingredient is conditional filtering. The authors argue that per-sample gradient utility is noisy, so filtering every batch aggressively can remove useful supervision. They first aggregate utilities at the batch level and compare the batch mean against recent history to determine whether the batch falls inside a moderate utility band. Batches inside the band are kept as-is. Only out-of-band batches trigger sample-level filtering, where interquartile-range thresholds are used to retain or discard examples within the batch. This design is meant to avoid overreacting to stochastic gradient noise while still rescuing good samples from otherwise weak batches.

Relative to common synthetic-data selection methods, FROST differs in three ways. It does not require a separate pretrained feature extractor for fidelity/diversity scoring, so it avoids expensive offline preprocessing of the full synthetic pool. It does not need a held-out validation set or an external judge, because the real training stream itself provides the anchor. And it is online: utility is recomputed as the model evolves, rather than assigned once in a static preprocessing stage.

From a pretraining perspective, the hidden assumption is that an EMA of real-data gradients is a stable proxy for the target objective. That seems plausible in moderate-scale fine-tuning, but it is less obvious in large mixed-corpus pretraining where gradient noise, domain conflict, and real/synthetic ratios can be very different.18:T621,The paper evaluates FROST on image classification, LLM fine-tuning for text-to-SQL, and a large industrial ads re-ranking system. On the public benchmarks, it filters out roughly 20% to 30% of synthetic data while outperforming training on the full synthetic pool.

The reported gains are 0.58% to 1.14% absolute accuracy improvement across three synthetic image generators, and 0.9% improvement on text-to-SQL fine-tuning. The industrial result is more telling in practical terms: using the full noisy synthetic pool causes a 0.211% relative NE regression compared with the real-only baseline, while FROST turns that into a 0.096% relative NE improvement. The authors note that gains around 0.02% are already considered meaningful in mature production recommenders, so the industrial effect size is not trivial.

Methodologically, the matched-drop-ratio comparison is important. The paper compares selection methods under the same synthetic-data discard rate, which makes the gains more attributable to better selection rather than simply using less data. Also worth checking is the ablation on batch-level gating plus sample-level filtering versus always-on per-sample filtering, since that is the part intended to control gradient-noise sensitivity.

The main caveat is scope. The LLM experiment is a downstream fine-tuning task, not large-scale language-model pretraining. The paper does not establish that real-anchored gradient utility remains stable or cost-effective for next-token pretraining with large synthetic corpora or reasoning-heavy synthetic mixtures.19:T4d9,For a skim read, start with the Introduction and Method to understand the logic of real-anchored utility and conditional filtering. Then read the text-to-SQL experiment and the main ablations. Around 20 to 30 minutes should be enough to decide whether the idea is portable to your own data pipeline.

Focus on four details. First, inspect how utility is computed in practice: full gradients, projected gradients, or some approximation. That determines scalability. Second, check how the real-gradient EMA is updated and stabilized, because the whole method depends on the anchor being reliable. Third, read the calibration rule for batch means and the IQR-based sample filtering, since that is where the paper tries to avoid over-filtering under noisy gradients. Fourth, look for behavior across different drop ratios, synthetic-data quality levels, and training stages.

If your interest is pretraining data rather than downstream fine-tuning, treat this as a prototype idea: use training signals instead of static data features to select synthetic data. Before scaling it up, the open questions are compute overhead, gradient approximation quality, and whether the real-gradient anchor remains meaningful under multi-domain mixed training.1a:T7c5,The formulation starts from minimum-token segmentation with a vocabulary budget. Each document is represented as a byte-level DAG whose edges are candidate substring occurrences. Byte edges are always available; multibyte edges are available only if the corresponding string is selected into the vocabulary. Given a vocabulary, minimum-count encoding is just a shortest path in the usable subgraph. The coupling difficulty is that selecting one token type enables all of its occurrences across the corpus.

The main idea is an occurrence-level Lagrangian relaxation. Each candidate occurrence gets a non-negative price lambda_e. On the document side, segmentation becomes a shortest-path problem with edge costs increased by these prices. On the vocabulary side, each token type accumulates the total bid of all its priced occurrences, and the lower bound subtracts the sum of the top-K bids allowed by the vocabulary budget. This yields a computable lower bound without a generic LP solver: shortest paths per document plus a global top-K selection over token bids. The paper argues that maximizing over prices recovers the LP relaxation, while validity of the reported bound is checked separately with an exact integer checker.

A useful extension is the boundary-licence formulation. Instead of only comparing the two endpoints—fully regex-constrained versus fully unrestricted—the method allows a budget on how many vocabulary entries may cross regex cuts. That produces a compression frontier and makes the design question continuous: how much compression can be recovered by permitting a small number of cross-boundary tokens.

The paper also keeps compression and prediction separate. Compression is analyzed through certified token-count intervals. Prediction is evaluated on held-out data with an explicit vocabulary and decoding protocol, because unrestricted vocabularies change token frequencies, context granularity, and effective predictability, not just sequence length.1b:T52e,The headline result on English Wikipedia is a certified boundary tax: regex boundaries increase the optimal token count by 28.3% to 36.8%. That is a large effect, showing that pre-tokenization boundaries materially constrain the compression optimum. BPE is only 2.1% above the constrained lower bound, which supports the claim that under a fixed regex regime BPE is already close to the best achievable compression. But BPE is 10.9% above the unrestricted lower bound, which explains why boundary-relaxing methods can still obtain substantially shorter sequences. These are not contradictory findings; they refer to different optimization problems.

The multilingual study covers 12 languages. Unrestricted fitted dictionaries compress better, but they have higher mean test bits-per-byte in every language. With independent tuning and evaluation seeds, the direction remains in 11 of 12 languages. This is the most practically relevant result for LM researchers: fewer tokens do not necessarily mean easier prediction or lower held-out loss.

The boundary-licence experiments are also important, even if the abstract only hints at them. They show how compression improves as a limited number of cross-boundary vocabulary entries are allowed, which is more informative than a binary constrained-versus-unrestricted comparison.1c:T605,This is a product announcement rather than a technical paper, so the training recipe is not disclosed and should not be over-inferred. Still, several technical directions are visible from the full text. First, Anthropic explicitly exposes effort level as a controllable inference-budget axis and compares models using score versus cost per task across effort settings. That implies joint design of model behavior and inference policy: low effort for throughput and low cost, higher effort for longer deliberation or more steps. Second, Sonnet 5.5 is repeatedly described as using fewer output tokens, doing less unnecessary web search, asking fewer blocking questions, and batching tool calls more often. Those are usually signs of post-training that shapes agent policy rather than simple prompting: when to call tools, whether to parallelize them, when to stop gathering information, and how aggressively to compress the response. Third, the claim that it improves without changing prompts suggests the gain is not prompt-specific tuning alone; the model’s internal preferences and action priors have shifted. Fourth, the safety note says its cyber capability is now comparable to Opus 5, which triggers stronger safeguards and fallbacks. That indicates capability growth has crossed a risk threshold, and release policy is coupled to capability evaluation. From a foundation-model perspective, the interesting object is the full stack: pretraining, agentic post-training, effort-controlled inference, tool-use policy, and safety gating.1d:T510,The most striking public number is 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 for Sonnet 5.5 versus 10.3% for Sonnet 5, a very large jump. The post also states that at Medium effort, Sonnet 5.5 exceeds Sonnet 5’s best score on Terminal-Bench for less than one-tenth of the cost per task. On FrontierCode, Sonnet 5.5 at High effort matches GPT-6 Sol’s best score at roughly one-fifth of the cost per task, and is 10 points above Sonnet 5 at the same effort while costing about one-fifteenth as much per task. On CursorBench, Sonnet 5.5 at Low effort beats Sonnet 5’s best score for under one-tenth of the cost, and its best score is within about two points of Opus 5.5. On AA-Briefcase, a long-horizon knowledge-work benchmark, Sonnet 5.5 at Medium effort beats Sonnet 5’s best score at about one-ninth of the cost. A frozen Qwen3-0.6B-Base encoder provides clean text states. Response states are corrupted in continuous space, and a bidirectional Transformer denoiser predicts clean states through velocity regression. The model also learns a token decoder, so the final response tokens are emitted in parallel. ELF-REG adds REPA+REG. REPA aligns intermediate denoiser states with hidden states from a frozen Qwen3-1.7B-Base AR teacher, using a learned projector and cosine loss at matching token positions. REG adds a global teacher-derived target: the last content-token state from the teacher is standardized, corrupted, and denoised as an extra token. This token exchanges information with text through self-attention and receives velocity-regression and REPA supervision. At inference time, the teacher and projector are removed; text states and the REG token start from noise, and only text is decoded. The paper also studies early stopping by decoding intermediate clean predictions before the full denoising trajectory finishes.20:T747,MoSAR, short for Mixture of Semantic Attention Regimes, inserts a lightweight router on the post-RoPE Q/K pathway. The router is bilinear and conditions on both queries and keys, rather than routing only one side. That choice is important: routing only queries gives row-wise structure, and routing only keys gives column-wise structure, but neither can localize useful two-dimensional regions of the attention matrix before dense similarities are computed. With both sides routed, the interaction between token i and token j selects a regime.

Each semantic regime defines a distance gate g(d). The gate is not just a simple exponential decay. It has a near-distance plateau where RoPE interactions are largely preserved, a transition region with smooth attenuation, and a low-relevance region where interactions become small enough to approximate away. This avoids the semantic discontinuity of hard local masks and makes approximability an outcome of the learned geometry.

The routing is input-conditioned and applied after positional encoding, so regime selection depends on contextual token representations that already carry positional structure. That is why the paper uses the term semantic regimes: locality is not determined by distance alone. MoSAR-Cost adds an explicit pressure toward shorter expected reach, biasing the router toward cheaper regimes and turning the quality-efficiency trade-off into a trainable objective.

Relative to prior efficient attention methods, the differences are clear. It does not predefine a sparse pattern; it predefines a set of decay laws and lets the data choose among them. It does not start by deleting edges; it first learns continuous attenuation and then exploits low-value regions for approximation. And it treats efficient attention as a geometry-learning problem rather than only an operator-design problem.21:T5f3,The main study uses 500M-parameter models trained from scratch and compares dense RoPE, fixed-locality baselines, MoSAR, and the cost-aware MoSAR-Cost. The headline result is that adaptive controlled decay outperforms both dense RoPE and fixed locality among the evaluated variants at 4096 and 8192 tokens, with MoSAR achieving the best perplexity in those long-context settings. The gains appear to be concentrated where long-range structure matters, which is aligned with the method’s goal.

The more interesting result is the inference-time approximation study. The authors replace soft mixture routing with deterministic top-1 routing at inference, effectively discretizing the learned geometry. This substantially reduces expected normalized reach while keeping perplexity competitive under length extrapolation. That suggests the learned regimes are not merely a training-time regularizer; they induce a geometry that can be compressed into a cheaper routing policy. MoSAR-Cost pushes the trade-off further toward lower reach, with some language-modeling cost, making the quality-versus-compute curve explicit rather than reporting a single operating point.

The most useful ablations are likely the ones on one-sided versus two-sided routing, number of regimes, the role of smooth transition regions, strength of cost regularization, and extrapolation behavior. The key question is not only whether perplexity improves, but whether perplexity, reach, and approximation error move in a stable and interpretable way.22:T412,Start with the introduction and lock onto the paper’s reframing: the target is not a better hand-designed sparse pattern, but a learned decay geometry over attention interactions. Then go to the method section and focus on three pieces: the definition of a semantic regime, the bilinear query-key router, and the MoSAR-Cost objective. It is worth understanding why routing is applied after RoPE rather than before it.

In the experiments, prioritize figures and tables that show perplexity across context lengths, expected or normalized reach, and the gap between soft mixture routing and deterministic top-1 routing. If time is limited, try to answer three questions: do the learned regimes actually separate into different locality behaviors, do those behaviors vary with layer and token semantics, and is the inference-time discretization loss small enough to matter in practice. Around 35 to 50 minutes should be enough for a solid skim. For replication judgment, the appendix on implementation details and extra ablations is necessary.23:T421,The analysis has three parts. First, it characterizes the population-optimal UDM predictor. Because uniform corruption mixes preserved tokens and random vocabulary tokens, every subset of observed positions defines a hypothesis about which context tokens are reliable. Time does not create new hypotheses; it reweights them through the noise level, with a signal-to-noise quantity such as rho_t = K alpha_t / (1 - alpha_t) controlling how much the observed context should be trusted. Second, the work studies the empirical finite-data oracle. In language data, the discrete sequence space is huge, and training examples are typically far apart. A corrupted sequence therefore remains closer to its original clean sequence than to competing examples over most noise levels, causing the posterior to concentrate and reducing the effect of time-dependent reweighting. Third, it derives a bound linking empirical time sensitivity to a post-corruption separation margin. The bound weakens near the high-noise endpoint, where multiple hypotheses become plausible.24:T4d5,LAVOIR builds on the Laya/Jev interface for typed decisions. The original input contains the question type, instruction, option markers, and the state. LAVOIR appends a slot block for candidate missing information. A single forward pass returns both the decision distribution and a predicted VOI score for each slot. The model keeps Laya’s ModernBERT-large decision head and adds a zero-initialized segment embedding so that, when no slots are present, the logits match Laya exactly in fp32. The VOI head reads each slot representation together with features of the current decision distribution and predicts a scalar value. It is a small MLP with about 0.27M parameters, LayerNorm, a 256-unit GELU hidden layer, and a scalar output. A Gini-based cap constrains the predicted value by the maximum expected gain of a calibrated posterior, which prevents the model from over-asking when it is already confident. Training labels are produced without human annotation: schema rules define the gold decision for complete profiles, an LLM verbalizes messages and answers, exact posteriors are computed by enumeration, and realized gains are measured as the increase in the model probability assigned to the gold decision after asking a slot.25:T4d9,LUDI changes the UDLM recipe in two places. First, it introduces a less uniform loss. The usual KL objective for UDLM matches the reverse transition to the exact posterior, but part of the objective encourages the prediction distribution to remain too uniform. With a large vocabulary, this weakens the clean-token signal and hurts few-step reverse generation. The authors simplify and approximate the original objective, decompose it into three terms, and remove the term that pushes predictions toward uniformity. The resulting loss drives each reverse transition more directly toward the clean token. Second, LUDI adds per-token time embeddings. A global diffusion time does not tell the model which individual positions are likely corrupted. Token-level time embeddings provide corruption hints for each position, letting the model identify reliable condition tokens and uncertain target tokens. This enables confidence-based sampling similar in spirit to masked diffusion models: generate easy or high-confidence tokens first, then use them as context for harder positions. Unlike MDLMs, LUDI keeps the uniform vocabulary prior rather than a mask-token prior. Unlike AR models, it does not force a strict left-to-right generation order.26:T534,The method, REST (REpresentation-Supervised Thoughts), augments the standard final-answer cross-entropy with four differentiable losses on the latent thought itself. The theoretical setup argues that CE on the final answer does not penalize bad intermediate representations as long as the correct answer remains sufficiently likely, so recursive systems can accumulate representational errors over rounds and across agents.

REST targets four properties. Causality requires the thought to preserve information needed to reproduce the correct output. Minimality pushes it to discard information irrelevant to that output. Separability prevents semantically distinct inputs, especially those with different output distributions, from collapsing to similar latent thoughts. Stability encourages the thought to reflect the distribution over plausible outputs rather than a single sampled answer trace. These losses are added to CE with tunable weights.

Implementation-wise, the paper studies both a multi-agent latent recursive system and a single-agent variant where a model feeds its own hidden states back as the next reasoning step. Importantly, REST does not change the architecture or inference procedure; it only changes the training objective. That makes the paper more about missing supervision than about a new system design.27:T432,The evaluation spans MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, AIME2025/2026, LiveCodeBench-v6, and MBPP+. Under matched training budget, identical training data, and the same latent budget, REST improves over CE-only by +3.5 points on average in the multi-agent setting and +3.3 in the single-agent setting. The best configurations reach +7.5 and +6.5 points, respectively. For a skim-level read, these are the main numbers to retain.

The paper also reports that REST decodes 15.4% more tokens on average at inference. The authors attribute this to a higher rate of convergence to a final answer. That is an interesting trade-off: better latent supervision improves accuracy, but not necessarily by reducing visible decoding cost in the current setup.

The analysis sections matter more than usual here. The paper claims that CE-only systems exhibit thought collapse and retention of irrelevant information, while REST-trained systems better satisfy the targeted properties. Those diagnostics are central to judging whether the method is doing more than adding another auxiliary loss.28:T4e1,The model follows the standard LoopLM decomposition: a Prelude P, a shared recurrent core F, and a Coda C, written as C ∘ F^K ∘ P during training. At inference, the number of recurrent applications can be changed to r. The study first uses minimalist LoopLMs under controlled pretraining settings, fixing effective training depth while varying the number of physical layers and recurrent loops. This isolates the effect of recurrence from total training depth. The paper then studies two design axes. The first is where non-recurrent computation should be placed. Output-side non-shared blocks help preserve knowledge behavior, especially when the model is under-unrolled, while input-side non-shared computation tends to help reasoning extrapolation. The second is how the recurrent core should be conditioned. Initial-state injection can hurt knowledge robustness when over-parameterized. The proposed history-state injection instead conditions on relative changes from intermediate states, giving the recurrent core access to trajectory information. Timestep conditioning lets the shared core behave differently at different loop indices. A lightweight channel-wise parameterization combines history-state injection and timestep conditioning.29:T42a,The experiments compare inference budgets below, at, and beyond the training horizon on both knowledge and reasoning tasks. A simple LoopLM can continue improving beyond its training horizon, and some configurations outperform non-recurrent counterparts under comparable training compute. The behavior is task-dependent: reasoning tasks can benefit from extra loops, while knowledge tasks may degrade. Harder reasoning examples do not consistently gain more from additional recurrence, which weakens the view that recurrence automatically allocates computation to difficult cases. Models with the same effective training depth but different physical-depth and loop-count configurations show different scaling curves. Ablations show that output-side non-recurrent blocks improve knowledge robustness under shallow unrolling, input-side blocks are more useful for reasoning extrapolation, and the joint conditioning design outperforms BaseLoop and the individual conditioning variants under extended inference budgets, with Fig. 7(c) serving as the central comparison.2a:T8ee,方法分成 TES 和 ACS 两条线。

TES，token-error supervision，在原生 router 之外增加一个轻量的 error head。这个 head 以共享的 token 表示为输入，为每个 expert 预测一个误差分数。然后用 native affinity 对这些 expert-wise error 做加权聚合，使聚合后的预测误差去拟合该 token 实际观察到的 next-token cross-entropy。训练好后，TES 不只是做一个辅助预测；它还在路由阶段把预测误差反馈到 expert 排序里：论文采用从 native affinity 中减去一个按比例缩放的 log-error 项，再做 top-K 选择。直观上，若某 expert 对当前 token 预测误差更高，就降低它被选中的相对优先级。这个设计保留了原有 top-K 稀疏预算，也不改 expert aggregation policy。

ACS，affinity-concentration supervision，则更克制。它不引入额外 head，也不在推理时改路由公式，而是直接用 realized token loss 去监督已选 expert 的归一化 affinity 概率的平方项。作者的解释是，这相当于根据 token loss 去调节路由分布该更尖锐还是更平坦：某些 token 上应更集中地押注少数 expert，另一些 token 上则不应过度集中。它是一个 headless 的对齐方式，参数和推理开销都更小。

监督目标上，论文主要用 Itakura–Saito divergence，也试了 ENLL。理论分析部分给出的关键结论是：对 TES 而言，两者都把聚合误差预测推向相同的期望目标，但对 LM 优化的梯度影响不同。若预测误差与真实误差一致，IS 不改变原始 CE 更新；ENLL 会相对放大低损失 token 的梯度权重。这个分析很重要，因为它说明“把 token error 接进 router”不是只有一个实现细节问题，而会改变训练动力学。

和已有方法相比，这篇工作不是重新设计一个全新 router，也不是增加更复杂的 expert selection 网络，而是在保留原生 MoE 结构和 top-K 预算的前提下，把 token-level error 作为显式监督接入路由。它的优点是兼容现有 backbone，改动小；局限是监督信号来自 realized CE，本身受当前模型状态影响，可能更适合 fine-tuning 或后期 router 校正，而未必直接适合早期大规模预训练。2b:T942,The method has two variants: TES and ACS.

TES, or token-error supervision, augments the native router with a lightweight error head. From the shared token representation, the head predicts an error score for each expert. These expert-wise predicted errors are then aggregated using the native affinity weights, and the aggregate is trained to match the realized next-token cross-entropy for that token. At inference and training time, TES does more than auxiliary prediction: it modifies expert ranking by subtracting a scaled log-error term from the native affinity before top-K selection. Intuitively, experts predicted to incur higher error are down-weighted in the routing decision. This preserves the original sparse execution budget and the architecture’s native expert aggregation policy.

ACS, or affinity-concentration supervision, is the lighter alternative. It adds no extra head and does not alter inference-time routing with an extra transformation. Instead, it directly supervises the squared probabilities of the normalized selected-expert affinities using the realized token loss. The effect is to encourage the routing distribution to become sharper or flatter depending on token difficulty. In other words, it shapes how concentrated the native router should be, without introducing a separate error predictor.

For supervision, the paper mainly uses Itakura-Saito (IS) divergence and also studies ENLL. The theoretical section is important. For TES, both objectives target the same expected token-error quantity, but they induce different optimization dynamics. When predicted and observed token error match, IS leaves the original CE update unchanged, whereas ENLL relatively upweights lower-loss tokens. That is a meaningful distinction: adding token-error supervision is not merely an auxiliary loss choice, but a change to how gradients are distributed.

Relative to prior MoE routing work, the contribution is not a new router architecture. It is a way to keep the native MoE design and top-K budget intact while explicitly supervising routing with token-level error. That makes the proposal easy to graft onto existing backbones. The likely limitation is that realized CE is itself model-state dependent, so the method may be better suited to fine-tuning or late-stage router correction than to the earliest phases of large-scale pretraining.2c:T525,Experiments are run on two backbones, Granite 3.1 and OLMoE-1B, across four multiple-choice QA benchmarks. The main comparisons are against standard CE fine-tuning and a parameter-matched Dual Affinity baseline.

On Granite, ACS-IS improves average accuracy by 2.1 points over CE fine-tuning with frozen native affinity. TES-IS improves over the parameter-matched Dual Affinity baseline by 2.3 points on Granite and 0.5 points on OLMoE, averaged across the four benchmarks. Under stronger supervision, TES reaches a 2.94-point gain on Granite ARC-Challenge.

These results support two conclusions. First, direct token-error supervision can improve routing in practice, not just in theory. Second, the better mechanism depends on the backbone and task: some settings benefit more from explicit error prediction, others from headless affinity shaping. The paper also keeps the native top-K execution budget unchanged in all variants, which matters for deployment realism.

From a pretraining perspective, the empirical scope is still limited. The paper does not show large-scale pretraining loss curves, routing stability during long runs, or how expert specialization evolves under these objectives. The evidence is therefore best read as a routing-supervision prototype rather than a validated MoE pretraining recipe.2d:T4bf,The method defines a Spectral Concentration Ratio over each pretrained weight matrix: the energy in the leading 10% singular directions is compared against the remaining spectrum, with regularization for small or rank-deficient cases. This concentration score is combined with the Frobenius norm to rank residual units by an offline sensitivity proxy. Each scheduled unit receives a lifetime. Before the lifetime expires, its residual branch is evaluated normally; after that, the executor reuses the cached residual-branch update from the latest refresh. A key design choice is that the method does not cache a stale full hidden state. The current upstream residual stream continues to flow through the identity path, and only the branch increment is reused. Dependency-coupled operations are grouped into atomic units. The perturbation analysis motivates the score for pre-norm Transformer attention and MLP branches by connecting spectral quantities to local Lipschitz-style sensitivity bounds. The authors explicitly limit this argument: drift along the diffusion trajectory, downstream amplification, AdaLN, U-shaped skips, cross-attention, and convolutional components are not fully captured by weights alone.2e:T8f8,方法由三个互补部件组成，全部是 training-free 的推理改造。

第一部分是 Token-Sparse Updates。作者先分析相邻 loop 之间 hidden state 的变化，发现后期只有少量 token 仍然发生显著更新，而且活跃 token 集合近似嵌套：后一轮还在变化的 token，大多是前一轮活跃 token 的子集。基于这个现象，FlashLoop 只对“活跃 token”重算 block，并为这些 token 生成新的 K/V；已经收敛的 token 直接复用上一轮状态和 KV。这样做同时减少了前向计算和跨 loop KV 存储。这里的关键不是静态剪枝，而是按 loop 动态决定哪些 token 继续更新。

第二部分是 Sparse Attention。作者观察到 attention output 的跨 loop 变化，主要由少数 attention columns 决定，也就是少量 key/value 位置主导了相邻 loop 的差异。这些重要列在相邻 loop 间还有较强稳定性，因此可以用前一轮的 attention-contribution 统计来预测下一轮需要重点计算的 key 集合。为了避免只在子集上做 softmax 带来的尺度偏移，方法还缓存全局概率质量，用来校正 sparse softmax 的归一化尺度。这个设计说明作者不是简单做 top-k attention，而是在尽量保留 full-softmax 数值语义的前提下近似跨 loop 增量。

第三部分是 KV-Residual Quantization。作者没有直接把每一轮完整 KV 都低比特量化，而是把某一轮作为 base state，再存相邻 loop 的低比特 residual。原因是实验显示相邻 loop 的 KV 残差比分别独立的完整 KV 更容易量化，在相同 bit-width 下重建误差更低。这一点很合理：循环 refinement 后，相邻状态差值分布更集中、更低熵。于是 KV cache 变成“量化基底 + 低比特残差”的形式，进一步压缩显存。

实现层面，论文强调这是 loop-native inference framework，而不是三个独立 trick 的拼接。作者做了 GPU 侧的 pipeline 和 kernel 优化，使 token 稀疏更新、稀疏 attention、残差量化能协同工作，避免稀疏带来的 kernel launch 和 gather/scatter 开销把理论收益吃掉。这个系统视角是论文成立的关键，因为 looped model 的瓶颈本来就不只在 FLOPs，还在 KV 带宽和长上下文内存。2f:T923,FlashLoop is a training-free inference framework built from three coordinated components.

The first is Token-Sparse Updates. The authors analyze hidden-state changes between adjacent loops and show that, as recurrence proceeds, only a small subset of tokens still changes substantially. Moreover, the active-token sets are approximately nested: tokens that remain active in a later loop are mostly a subset of those active in the previous one. FlashLoop therefore recomputes the Transformer block only for active tokens and reuses hidden states and KV states for tokens that have effectively converged. This reduces both compute and the need to maintain a full per-loop KV cache.

The second is Sparse Attention. The paper shows that cross-loop changes in attention outputs are dominated by a sparse subset of attention columns, meaning a small number of key/value positions account for most of the difference between adjacent loops. These important columns are relatively stable across loops, so FlashLoop predicts them using attention-contribution statistics from the previous loop. To avoid the scale mismatch that usually appears when softmax is computed on a subset, the method caches global probability mass to preserve the normalization scale of the full softmax. This is more careful than a generic top-k attention approximation; it is tailored to incremental cross-loop updates.

The third is KV-Residual Quantization. Instead of quantizing each loop’s full KV states independently, FlashLoop stores a quantized base state plus low-bit residuals between adjacent loops. The motivation is empirical: adjacent-loop KV residuals are easier to quantize than full KV tensors, yielding lower reconstruction error under the same bit budget. That matches the intuition that iterative refinement makes successive states highly correlated and low-entropy in difference space.

A key part of the paper is that these are not presented as isolated tricks. The system is implemented with GPU-aware pipelining and optimized kernels so that token sparsity, sparse attention, and residual quantization work together without losing the gains to irregular memory access or kernel overhead. That systems angle is essential because the bottleneck in looped inference is not just FLOPs, but also KV bandwidth and memory footprint under long context.30:T5ee,The motivating numbers are striking. On a single A100 with a 32K-token prompt, Ouro-2.6B with four loops takes 27 seconds for prefill, while LLaMA-3.1-8B takes 3 seconds. KV cache alone is about 48 GiB for Ouro versus 4 GiB for LLaMA. The point is clear: a smaller looped model can be much worse in latency and memory if executed in the standard dense way.

Across several looped Transformer models, FlashLoop reports up to 1.64x end-to-end speedup and up to 6x KV-cache memory reduction while largely preserving accuracy. The paper’s main message is not extreme compression at any cost, but recovering the practical efficiency that parameter sharing was supposed to provide in the first place.

The most informative experiments are the mechanism studies. Figure 2 and the appendix document three empirical regularities: token updates become increasingly sparse across loops and form approximately nested active sets; attention-output differences are concentrated in a small number of columns that can be predicted from the previous loop; and KV residuals are more quantization-friendly than full KV states under matched settings. These analyses justify why each module should work, instead of treating the speedup as a black-box engineering result.

From a research perspective, the important takeaway is not only the 1.64x number. It is the evidence that additional loop depth does not translate into fully new computation at every step; a meaningful fraction of it becomes reusable, predictable, and compressible.31:T4bd,For a skim-level read, start with the Introduction, Figure 1, and Figure 2. Then read the method subsections for the three components and finish with the main results and ablations. Around 25 to 40 minutes should be enough to capture the main ideas.

Three things deserve attention. First, look at how the paper measures cross-loop redundancy, especially token-update sparsity and the nested active-set pattern. That determines whether Token-Sparse Updates is a robust structural property or just a one-off observation. Second, inspect the normalization correction in Sparse Attention, namely how cached global probability mass is used to preserve softmax scale. If this part is weak, accuracy usually degrades quickly. Third, check the KV-residual quantization error curves and bit-width choices; that section is particularly useful for long-context inference and serving work.

Even if your main focus is pretraining rather than inference systems, there is a deeper question worth keeping in mind: why do looped models naturally exhibit lazy updates? The paper does not fully answer it, but the phenomenon may connect to iterative refinement, residual-state convergence, and stabilization of attention patterns.32:T41b,The method defines the original routed MoE output for a token as a consensus, meaning the weighted mixture to be preserved, not an assumption that experts agree. Each expert is represented through its residual relative to this consensus. For a fixed layer input, RAZOR derives an exact single-deletion identity for the local output change. The identity accounts for survivor weight renormalization and, when applicable, router-selected refill that promotes an unselected expert into the active set. Without refill, the deletion shift depends on the deviation between the removed expert output and the consensus, scaled by its routing weight; this already shows why gate mass and output norm are insufficient. With refill, the promoted expert’s residual can compensate for or amplify the removed contribution. RAZOR runs only forward passes on calibration tokens, aggregates local deletion damage per expert within each layer, and prunes the most replaceable experts under the target budget. It avoids gradients, subset search, and recovery training.33:T4dd,The paper uses a roofline-style analysis to separate weight traffic from KV-cache traffic during decode. For a model with P parameters and weight width wp, a batch-one decode step performs roughly 2P FLOPs and reads P·wp bytes, giving about 1 FLOP/B for BF16 weights. An H100 SXM has a BF16 dense ridge point around 295 FLOP/B, so this regime is bandwidth-bound by a large margin. KV attention has the same structure: one query attending over s cached tokens costs about 4sdh FLOPs per head and reads 2sdh·wkv bytes, again about 1 FLOP/B in BF16. GQA improves reuse by the query-to-KV head group factor g, but even g=8 gives only about 8 FLOP/B, still far below the ridge point. The paper then explains why batching helps weight reads but not KV reads. Weight bytes can be amortized across requests; KV bytes cannot, because each sequence owns its cache. The techniques are organized into five mechanism classes: quantization reduces element width, token eviction reduces retained tokens, paging manages KV blocks and fragmentation, prefix caching shares common prompt prefixes, and memory tiering moves KV state across HBM, host DRAM, and storage. The paper’s comparison discipline is to keep analytical claims and measured claims separate.34:T422,The most important quantitative examples are concrete. For Llama-3-70B in BF16, the weight footprint is about 140 GB, already larger than a single 80 GB HBM device. The KV cache size is Bkv = 2·L·nkv·dh·wkv·s. With L=80, nkv=8, dh=128, and BF16 storage, Llama-3-70B uses 327,680 KV bytes per token. A single 128k-token sequence therefore adds about 42 GB of KV state; a 1M-token sequence requires about 328 GB, more than the aggregate HBM of four 80 GB H100 devices. The arithmetic-intensity numbers are equally important: BF16 batch-one decode sits near 1 FLOP/B for weight traffic, while the H100 ridge point is about 295 FLOP/B. On the attention side, GQA with group factor 8 still reaches only about 8 FLOP/B. Weight-side batching approaches the ridge only at a batch size around 295 in this simplified model, while KV-side intensity is invariant to batch size. The paper’s measurement contribution is to make these comparisons explicit rather than mixing throughput, latency, memory footprint, and quality degradation under incompatible settings.35:T45c,The analysis separates two mechanisms. Feedback exposure describes where quantization error is structurally dangerous. In models such as Huginn-3.5B and Recurrent-Llama, recurrence passes through a non-residual loop-entry adapter. Quantizing this adapter perturbs the recurrent state without an identity path, so the error is injected into future steps. Quantizing the residual core is much less harmful because the identity path buffers the perturbation. The paper uses the local spectral radius of the per-step Jacobian as a stability diagnostic for possible amplification directions. Calibration blindness is a different issue. GPTQ builds a Hessian proxy H=X^T X from calibration activations. If X is collected only from the first invocation of a shared layer, it can miss directions that appear in later loop steps. The paper compares this one-step calibration with trajectory calibration, which accumulates activations across all recurrent invocations. It also distinguishes per-channel INT4 from grouped INT4 with group size 128, where the latter reduces quantization error at the cost of extra scale storage.36:T4c7,The Huginn-3.5B diagnostic is the clearest result. On 100 GSM8K examples, bf16 reaches 34% exact match, while per-channel INT4 on both the loop-entry adapter and recurrent core drops to 0%. A 50-prompt token-agreement diagnostic localizes the damage: adapter-only INT4 gives 10.5% agreement, adapter plus core gives 10.6%, and core-only INT4 keeps 87.9%. This points to the non-residual adapter as the main failure point. COCONUT behaves differently because it reuses a residual GPT-2 stack; agreement increases from 44.8% after the base forward to 61.5% after eight latent recurrences. Standard one-step sensitivity metrics fail to predict the Huginn result: small random input perturbations rank the adapter as the least sensitive among 17 projections, and Hessian trace highlights a core projection even though quantizing the adapter is far more damaging. Grouped INT4 avoids the immediate collapse, but one-step GPTQ still underperforms round-to-nearest on five of nine checkpoints. More calibration prompts do not remove the mismatch, because the missing information is the set of directions visited later in the trajectory. Linear-filter and Mamba controls show that feedback exposure is not specific to Transformers.37:T85b,The method has three main components. First, it redefines the reusable object. Instead of caching whole requests or token prefixes, DynBranch stores a completed branch subgraph together with the exact input that triggered it and the external reads it depended on. A later request may consume the entry only if the input matches exactly and those reads are still fresh; any write to the recorded dependencies invalidates the entry. This is important for agent workflows where retrieval and tool outputs depend on mutable external state, so prompt matching alone is insufficient.

Second, it makes unresolved branches addressable. The mechanism relies on a stable coordinate provided by the workflow template: the identity of a decision point known before the branch resolves, such as a router stage or a fixed tool-selection site. Using this coordinate, the system can launch candidate branch subgraphs as fills during the resolution window. A fill is speculative execution of a candidate downstream subgraph before the actual branch is chosen. The safety rule is strict: fills remain invisible until branch selection occurs and a canonical demand authorizes their use via exact match and freshness checks. Wrong predictions therefore waste resources but do not alter semantics.

Third, DynBranch uses a two-level admission controller. One level decides whether to generate candidates at all; the second decides whether each candidate fill should run. The decision criterion is whether expected benefit exceeds a load-dependent price. That price is not a fixed threshold. It reads current decode occupancy and KV occupancy from the engine and prices work over the fill's execution horizon. This allows aggressive speculation at low load and automatic contraction at high load. The paper also indicates that the controller learns benefit estimates from delayed feedback rather than relying only on static heuristics.

Implementation-wise, DynBranch sits at the model-API boundary between agent harnesses and unmodified SGLang or vLLM backends. That makes it a serving middleware design rather than a new agent runtime or a model-side method.38:T737,The main setup uses Qwen3-32B on 4×H200, with additional results on Qwen3-8B with an RTX 4090. The paper first motivates the problem empirically: in measured coding, research, and scientific agents, 45%–57% of end-to-end latency is downstream time serialized after model output. That establishes that the branch-resolution barrier is not a corner case.

On performance, DynBranch reduces mean latency by up to 32% relative to the strongest prior system for each workload on the same GPUs, and by 46%–66% relative to a no-reuse floor. When reuse is disabled and only early fill is kept, mean latency still drops by 8.5%–34.4% on model-driven paths, and user-turn latency drops by 46.6%–47.7% in human-interaction settings. This is an important result: the gains do not come only from cross-request reuse; overlapping work during the branch-resolution window already matters.

The experimental structure also suggests three points worth checking closely. First is correctness: the paper states that workflow results are preserved, consistent with the design where speculative fills become visible only after canonical authorization. Second is load sensitivity: the two-level controller should show different admission behavior under different occupancy regimes, otherwise the claim of safe speculation under load would be weak. Third is generality: the authors report that benefits persist across backbone families, which suggests the effect comes from workflow structure and serving dynamics rather than a model-specific artifact.

The provided text does not include the full result tables, so it is not safe to invent more workload-level absolute latency or hit-rate numbers. But the central empirical message is clear: the combination of reuse, early fill, and load-aware admission outperforms caching-only or speculation-only baselines.39:T525,The framework maximizes draft-token acceptance subject to an f-divergence constraint between the mentored output distribution and the target distribution. The total-variation case is used as a warm-up and has a clean geometric structure: the set of optimal solutions is the intersection of a coordinate-wise hyperrectangle induced by the drafter and target, the probability simplex, and the active divergence boundary. This set is large enough to contain the optimal solutions for all strictly convex f-divergences. For a general strictly convex f-divergence, the optimal mentored distribution is unique and has a coordinate-wise clamping form, π* = max{αq, min{p, βq}}, where q is the target distribution, p is the drafter distribution, and 0 ≤ α < 1 < β. Intuitively, each token probability is kept within lower and upper multiplicative bands around the target probability, while moving along a one-dimensional path from the target toward the drafter. A notable property is that this path does not depend on the chosen f-divergence. The paper further connects the composite output distribution to boosting by developing a multiclass extension of self-normalized boosting and by showing how the drafter-target mixture can satisfy boosting-style conditions when the two models have useful edge complementarity.3a:T4fb,The method, PISA, builds a coarse-to-fine pyramid over key blocks. The finest level contains fixed-size blocks, and each coarser level is formed by pooling adjacent lower-level representations. Instead of scoring every fine-grained block, routing starts at the coarsest level. At each level, the query computes LogSumExp scores over only a bounded candidate set, keeps the Top-K candidates, and expands those selected blocks into their children at the next finer level. This repeats until the leaf blocks are reached.

With a fixed branching factor, Top-K budget, and leaf block size, each query evaluates only a bounded number of candidates per level, and the number of levels is O(log N). That gives O(log N) routing per query and O(N log N) routing over the sequence. The final sparse attention is then computed over the selected original blocks.

The practical angle is important here. The authors implement hardware-aware Triton kernels that fuse multi-level routing and LSE scoring, so intermediate candidates do not need to be repeatedly materialized and moved through memory. They also avoid constructing a dense query-key score matrix. That matters because many sparse-attention ideas fail to deliver real speedups once kernel and memory traffic are taken seriously.3b:T91f,方法核心是 acoustic-to-text KV compression。基础模型是 MiniCPM-o 4.5，它按 1 秒为单位处理 duplex unit，每个 unit 内包含音频 token、一个 native 的 <|listen|> 或 <|speak|> 决策，以及后续可能的响应生成。作者在每个 unit 的第一个 native decision 之后，插入一个可选的 transcription segment，用新引入的 <|asr_start|> 和 <|asr_end|> 包围。这个 segment 只作为语言模型上下文中的文本记忆存在，不送入 speech decoder，也不会被说出来。

推理时，模型自己决定是否打开 side channel。如果预测出 <|asr_start|>，就贪心解码最多 64 个文本 token，直到 <|asr_end|>；若超长或遇到控制 token，则强制闭合。随后，当 resident KV cache 超过目标预算时，系统驱逐更早的 acoustic states，但保留这些 transcript token，并保留一个最近的 acoustic window 以覆盖转写延迟。于是，较老的语音内容以文本形式留在上下文里，最近一段仍保留原始声学细节，形成“远处文本化、近处声学化”的混合记忆。

训练上，作者没有单独接一个 ASR 模型，而是复用原有 LM backbone，只用 LoRA 适配 side channel。监督信号来自带词级强制对齐的转写数据：每个词根据其声学结束时间和额外延迟 δ 被分配到某个 1 秒 unit 中，每个词只出现在一个目标 transcription segment。仅用 transcription cross-entropy 会改变原模型的原生对话行为，所以作者再加入 token-level knowledge distillation。具体做法是：冻结原始 full-duplex 模型作为 teacher，让它在同一音频上、但不插入 transcription segment 地运行；收集 teacher 在所有 native prediction positions 的全词表分布；student 在插入 transcription segment 的序列上训练时，对这些 native 位置同时拟合 teacher 分布。这样 side channel 学会转写，同时尽量不扰动原有 listen/speak 决策、停顿处理、打断响应等行为。

这个设计和“单独训练一个流式 ASR，再把文本喂回模型”相比，有两个差异。其一，推理时不需要额外 ASR 模块，部署更简单；其二，蒸馏约束的是 full-duplex 原生行为，而不只是转写准确率，因此目标更贴近语音对话模型的系统需求。3c:T828,实验围绕三件事展开：KV 峰值控制、长时语音理解、实时性与交互行为保持。主模型是 MiniCPM-o 4.5。作者指出，转写后的文本记忆大约每秒只占 3 个序列位置，而原始 acoustic history 约占 17 个位置，这给压缩上限提供了直观背景。

在十分钟 LongSpeech session 上，与“同样经过 side-channel 适配但不做 eviction”的模型相比，峰值 streaming KV cache 大小下降 64.6%。这说明收益主要来自“文本化后驱逐旧声学 KV”，而不是仅仅插入 transcript token。长时理解方面，论文称该方法在 transcription、temporal question answering、summarization 上都优于 native streaming，说明文本记忆不仅节省显存，也改善了对长程语言内容的保持。

实时性方面，在 4K KV cache budget 下，包含 transcription 与 cache eviction 在内的整套处理，在 H100、batch size 1 上对每个 1 秒音频单元平均耗时 461 ms；在 10,039 个 unit 的测量中没有 deadline miss。这一点很关键，因为方法成立的前提就是 side channel 能在 listening-time slack 内完成。若超过 1 秒窗口，就会破坏 full-duplex 实时性。

行为保持方面，Full-Duplex-Bench 上 pause-handling、turn-taking、interruption 等指标与原模型相当，支持了蒸馏约束确实在抑制 side-channel 训练对原生交互行为的扰动。摘要还提到 WER 统计会把 skipped/truncated segments 计入错误，这意味着作者没有通过只评估成功打开 side channel 的片段来美化结果。

从方法设计推断，值得关注的消融应包括：只做 CE 转写监督、不做 KD 时 native behavior 的退化；不同 KV budget 下理解与实时性的折中；recent acoustic window 大小对性能的影响；以及 emission delay δ 对转写完整性和驱逐时机的影响。给出的全文片段没有完整表格数字，但主结论已经足够明确：在线文本化旧语音上下文，可以在不破坏 full-duplex 交互的前提下显著降低峰值 KV，并提升长时理解。3d:T95a,The core method is acoustic-to-text KV compression. The base model, MiniCPM-o 4.5, processes interaction in 1-second duplex units. Each unit contains audio tokens, a native <|listen|> or <|speak|> decision, and possibly response generation. After the first native decision in each unit, the authors insert an optional transcription segment delimited by two new tokens, <|asr_start|> and <|asr_end|>. This segment stays in the language-model context as textual memory, but it is excluded from the speech decoder input and from spoken output.

At inference time, the model decides whether to open the side channel. If it predicts <|asr_start|>, it greedily decodes up to 64 text tokens until <|asr_end|>; if the segment overruns or hits a control token, the segment is forcibly closed. When the resident KV cache exceeds a target budget, older acoustic states are evicted while transcript tokens are retained, together with a recent acoustic window that covers transcription delay. The resulting memory is hybrid: older context is preserved in text form, while recent context remains acoustically grounded.

Training avoids a separate ASR model. The side channel is adapted with LoRA on top of the existing LM backbone. Supervision comes from transcribed utterances with word-level forced alignment. Each word is assigned to a 1-second unit based on its acoustic endpoint plus an additional emission delay delta, and each word appears in exactly one target transcription segment. However, pure transcription cross-entropy would alter the model's native conversational behavior. To prevent that, the paper adds token-level knowledge distillation. A frozen teacher, namely the original full-duplex model without transcription segments, processes the same audio. Its full-vocabulary distributions at native prediction positions are collected, and the student is trained to match them at those positions while also learning the inserted transcription segments. This constrains changes to native listen/speak decisions, pause handling, interruption behavior, and response generation.

Compared with a pipeline that runs a separate streaming ASR and feeds text back into the model, this design has two practical differences. It removes the need for an extra ASR module at inference, and it regularizes the adapted model toward preserving full-duplex behavior rather than optimizing transcription alone.3e:T989,The experiments focus on three aspects: peak KV control, long-form speech understanding, and real-time behavioral preservation. The base model is MiniCPM-o 4.5. The paper notes that transcript memory uses roughly 3 sequence positions per second of speech, versus about 17 for acoustic history, which gives a clear intuition for why the compression can matter.

On 10-minute LongSpeech sessions, peak streaming KV cache size is reduced by 64.6% relative to the same side-channel-adapted model without eviction. This is an important comparison because it isolates the gain from converting old acoustic context into text and then evicting acoustic KV, rather than from simply inserting transcript tokens. On long-form understanding, the method improves transcription, temporal question answering, and summarization over native streaming, suggesting that textual memory is not only cheaper but also more effective for retaining long-range linguistic content.

On real-time feasibility, under a 4K KV-cache budget the full processing path, including transcription and cache eviction, averages 461 ms per 1-second audio unit on an H100 at batch size 1. Across 10,039 measured units, there are no deadline misses. This matters because the whole method depends on finishing side-channel work within the listening-time slack.

On behavioral preservation, results on Full-Duplex-Bench show comparable pause handling, turn taking, and interruption performance. That supports the claim that token-level distillation successfully constrains the side-channel adaptation. The paper also states that skipped or truncated transcription segments are counted as errors in WER, which is a useful detail because it avoids reporting only successful side-channel openings.

The most informative ablations are likely the following: cross-entropy-only transcription training versus CE plus KD, to show how native behavior degrades without distillation; different KV budgets to expose the trade-off between memory and understanding; the size of the retained recent acoustic window; and the effect of the emission delay delta on transcription completeness and eviction timing. Start with the Introduction to set the boundary correctly: the goal is not better ASR, but online memory compression inside a full-duplex speech LM. Then read the method section carefully, focusing on where the transcription segment is inserted, how the side channel is opened during inference, and how eviction is triggered. Those details determine whether the approach is actually deployable without changing the backbone architecture.

The training section is worth extra attention. In particular, look at how forced alignment assigns words to units and how token-level KD is applied only at native prediction positions. That is the most technically interesting part, because it explains why LoRA adaptation can add transcription ability without noticeably damaging native listening and speaking behavior.

In the experiments, prioritize the tables on peak KV usage, LongSpeech understanding tasks, and Full-Duplex-Bench behavior preservation. If there is a latency timeline or a budget sweep, read that too, since it directly shows engineering feasibility. Around 30–40 minutes should be enough for the key ideas. If you only want to judge transferability to another speech LM, read the method figure, the training objective, and the real-time result under the 4K budget.40:T7d2,The method has three layers. First, the paper builds an error model for MLA dual-path quantization. MLA stores a shared low-rank content latent and a decoupled RoPE key cache. Quantization errors in the content path propagate through attention matching, value aggregation, and their interaction. Errors in the RoPE path enter mainly through the RoPE-induced QK logit term. Across six models from four families, the authors show that under matched cache reconstruction error, RoPE-path quantization causes substantially larger attention-output distortion. They then explain this with an operator–error model based on attention sensitivity to logits, how quantization error energy is allocated across subspaces, and how error directions couple with sensitive operator directions.

Second, they propose QuantMLA, a function-aligned dual-path quantization framework. The key design choice is not to use one shared quantization objective. Instead, each path gets its own offline-fusible transformation space and its own functional target. For the content path, the objective is attention-output reconstruction: optimize the quantized representation so that the downstream attention output is preserved, rather than merely reconstructing the latent tensor. For the RoPE path, the objective is positional QK reconstruction: directly preserve the position-sensitive QK term, since that is the main route through which RoPE errors affect outputs. The paper also derives a theoretical bound linking this objective to output distortion.

Third, the paper includes a native low-bit MLA attention backend. Unpacking and dequantization are fused into the attention computation instead of restoring high-precision tensors first. This matters because cache compression only translates into real serving gains if bandwidth and intermediate memory traffic are reduced at execution time. The evaluation therefore includes not only kernel-level behavior but also end-to-end vLLM serving under the same scheduling policy.41:T5cf,The analysis spans six models from four MLA families, with total model sizes ranging from 16B to 1T parameters. The main empirical results are threefold.

First, the paper reports what it describes as the first joint INT4 caching result for both the content cache and the RoPE cache in MLA, with only minor accuracy degradation. That is the central quality result, because prior MLA quantization work largely avoided low-bit RoPE caching. Second, in a more aggressive setting, it further compresses the content cache to INT2 while keeping the RoPE cache at INT4, and still maintains competitive performance on difficult reasoning and coding benchmarks. This supports the paper’s main analysis: the content path is materially more compressible than the RoPE path. Third, on the systems side, it reports up to 3.59× KV-cache compression at 128K context length and up to 5.168× whole-job output throughput relative to BF16 in the evaluated cache-pressure workload under the same native vLLM scheduling policy.

The most useful ablations are not just score tables. They establish a chain of evidence: matched reconstruction error does not imply matched functional distortion; path-specific objectives outperform generic reconstruction objectives; and a native low-bit backend is necessary to realize the memory savings as actual throughput gains. The full benchmark-by-benchmark numbers are not fully visible in the provided text snippet, but the main trends and claimed gains are clear.42:T4aa,Read it in three passes: mechanism, method, then system. Then move to the QuantMLA design, especially the path-specific transformation spaces and the two different functional objectives. The paper first shows that early draft positions already contain recoverable token-predictive information in shallow layers, and that successor accuracy depends strongly on both the adjacent predecessor content and the depth at which that information is introduced. DSpine uses a gated adjacent injection module at every layer: each position writes its predicted feature into the next position, so the causal chain unfolds over network depth while all draft positions are updated in parallel. Layer-wise output-embedding supervision encourages shallow layers to form transferable predictive features. It defines a token’s phase as its relative position inside a compression window, usually position modulo the compression stride. The authors use a code-completion probe where only the length of a decorative prefix changes; the model’s preferred next token flips with the compression period. They then run controlled needle-in-a-haystack retrieval while sweeping the source phase. To test causality, they pretrain a family of Qwen3-0.6B-style transformers where KV compression is the main architectural change, including variants that use simple averaging inside each window. Compressed models show stride-matched periodicity, while full-attention baselines do not. The paper then goes beyond the boundary explanation. Splitting a key-value pair across windows hurts retrieval, but large variation remains even when the pair stays inside one window. An idealized induction task explains why this can arise: mixing several tokens into a query-agnostic compressed memory weakens later key-query matching, and gradient flow can push gates toward selective retention of particular phases.46:T469,LatentSift replaces the first-stage LLM-based execution-free verifier in a hybrid SWE verification pipeline. The standard pipeline scores all K trajectories with an EF verifier, keeps a subset, then applies regression tests, LLM-generated tests, and a final EF selection step. LatentSift instead collects hidden states while the policy is generating candidates, adding no extra LLM tokens. It represents each trajectory through three channels: reasoning states, environment-observation states, and function-call states. During training, states from successful and unsuccessful trajectories are stored in positive and negative banks. At inference time, candidate states are compared with these banks, step-level distance margins are aggregated, and channel-level ranks are fused conservatively so that a candidate must look good across the behavioral channels. A separate linear scorer trained on policy hidden states produces a learned trajectory score. The final filtering score combines normalized ranks from the distance branch and the learned scorer, then retains half of the candidates for the remaining verification stages.47:T91b,方法由三部分组成，分别对应作者提出的三个瓶颈。

第一部分是 path-aware tile routing。DFlash 原生实现对 prefill 和 verify 复用同一套 attention tile 选择逻辑，但两者 query length 分布完全不同：prefill 往往很长，verify 只有短 candidate block。沿用 prefill 的 tile 会让 verify 阶段出现大量无效 padding。DScale 为不同执行路径选择预编译 tile，使 verify 使用更贴合短序列 workload 的 tile 形状，同时保留 prefill 的复用收益。这里的关键不是新 attention 算法，而是把“prefill 和 verify 是两种不同 kernel workload”显式编码进图选择逻辑。

第二部分是 dynamic verify-length, DVL。作者不去缩短 drafter 的生成长度，而是在验证前决定每个请求实际送多少 candidate prefix 进入 target verify graph。为此训练了一个很小的 predictor，参数量只有 112K，针对 target–drafter pair 学一次即可。它不做概率校准，也不需要硬件 profile，只输出用于排序/分配的分数。系统在共享预算下给不同请求分配不同 verify-length，并把总 candidate-slot 容量压到 native verify graph 的一半左右。这样做的动机很清楚：真正值得 target 花算力验证的，是更可能形成长 accepted prefix 的请求；对低潜力请求，保留完整 draft 但少送一些位置去 verify，比一刀切截断所有请求更划算。

第三部分是 fixed-address compact workspace。DVL 之后，每个请求的 prefix 边界会动态变化，这与 CUDA graph 偏好的 fixed-shape 接口冲突。DScale 用固定地址工作区来承载压缩后的 token、边界和前缀信息，让 decision graph、verify graph 和 acceptance 逻辑共享这些动态边界，同时继续复用 captured graphs，而不需要 CPU 侧重新切片。论文里 flat-pack compaction 是这里的配套机制：把各请求选中的 prefix 紧凑排布进共享验证预算，尽量保留长前缀，减少 padding 和空槽。

整体上，DScale 的思路不是改 acceptance rule，也不是训练更强 drafter，而是把 verify 当成一个受预算约束的 packing 和调度问题。相比 DSpark 这类依赖 confidence calibration 和硬件曲线的方法，它更轻量，也更容易迁移到已有 DFlash 部署上。48:T9d9,The method has three main components, each tied to one of the identified bottlenecks.

First, path-aware tile routing. Native DFlash uses the same attention-tile selection logic for prefill and verification, even though the workloads are structurally different: prefill has long query lengths, while verification operates on short candidate blocks. Reusing prefill-oriented tiles in verification leaves many inactive positions and wastes work. DScale introduces path-specific routing over precompiled tiles so that verification uses tile shapes better matched to short-query execution, while prefill still benefits from its own optimized path. This is not a new attention algorithm; it is a workload-aware graph-selection strategy.

Second, dynamic verify-length allocation (DVL). Instead of shortening the drafter’s output, DScale decides how many candidate positions from each request should actually enter the target verification graph. A tiny predictor—112K parameters, trained once per target–drafter pair—produces scores for allocation. The predictor does not require confidence calibration and does not depend on hardware speed-curve preparation. Under a shared verification budget, requests with higher expected acceptance potential receive longer verified prefixes, while lower-value prefixes are trimmed. The total candidate-slot budget is reduced to roughly half of the native verification capacity. The point is to spend target-model verification on prefixes likely to yield longer accepted runs, rather than uniformly truncating every request.

Third, a fixed-address compact workspace. DVL makes request boundaries dynamic, which conflicts with fixed-shape graph replay. DScale introduces a compact workspace that stores packed tokens, boundaries, and prefix metadata at fixed addresses, allowing the decision graph, verification graph, and acceptance logic to share changing boundaries while still reusing captured graphs. Flat-pack compaction is the associated packing mechanism: selected prefixes from different requests are laid out densely under the shared budget, preserving long useful prefixes and reducing padding without CPU-side re-slicing.

Overall, DScale treats verification as a budgeted packing and scheduling problem. It does not modify the acceptance rule and does not depend on a stronger drafter. Compared with approaches such as DSpark that rely on confidence calibration and hardware profiling, it is lighter-weight and easier to layer onto an existing DFlash-style deployment.49:T60e,The evaluation spans four datasets, two target models, and concurrency levels from 8 to 32 on A100-40GB with tensor parallelism 1. Relative to DFlash, DScale improves geometric-mean throughput by 43.9% to 48.8% and reduces aggregate mean end-to-end latency by 31.4% to 33.1%. On GSM8K, GPU profiling shows 30.8% to 52.5% shorter complete decode steps.

A particularly informative intermediate metric is accepted-token retention. If verification capacity is reduced without a good allocation policy, only about 71% of accepted tokens are retained. With budget adjustment, retention rises to above 91%. That result matters because it shows the gain is not simply from verifying fewer tokens; it comes from verifying fewer low-value tokens while preserving most generation progress.

The ablations are the strongest part of the empirical section. The paper presents cumulative ablations showing that path-aware tiles, predictor scoring, budget allocation, and packing/workspace each add incremental benefit rather than one trick dominating the outcome. Runtime overhead is also small: prediction, budget allocation, and packing together account for only 3.08% to 4.08% of step time in GPU execution at concurrency 8. The motivation section provides the key baseline profile: for Qwen3-8B with an approximately 1B, five-layer DFlash drafter on GSM8K at concurrency 16, 83.3% of summed GPU-kernel time is spent in the target verification graph, versus 10.9% in the draft graph. That profile explains why verification-side optimization is the right target.4a:T4b7,Read this as a systems paper about where block-diffusion decoding actually spends time. Start with the introduction and background, especially the native DFlash profile showing that verification dominates GPU kernel time. Without that profile, the rest of the design can look like engineering detail; with it, the design choices become well motivated.

Then follow the three challenges and their paired mechanisms. For path-aware tile routing, the key question is why prefill and verification should not share the same tile policy. For DVL, focus less on the predictor architecture and more on how the paper formulates per-request verified-prefix length as a shared-budget allocation problem. For the compact workspace, the important point is how dynamic boundaries are propagated through fixed-shape graph replay without falling back to CPU re-slicing.

In the experiments, prioritize the cumulative ablations and the accepted-token-retention plots. Those figures show that DScale is not buying throughput by aggressively truncating useful work. If you only want a quick decision on relevance, read the baseline profile, the DVL section, and the main results table. Estimated reading time: 25–35 minutes.4b:T6ee,The method, BASE, stands for Batch-Aware Selection of Experts using Predicted Removal Error. For token t, the MoE output is y_t = sum_{u in R_t} w_{t,u} E_u(z_t). If some experts are not loaded at the batch level, the layer output changes. The paper writes the resulting squared error as a sum of individual removal terms plus cross terms between experts omitted together. The key claim is that selection is robust to dropping the cross terms, which makes it possible to score experts independently and keep the highest-scoring ones under a fixed budget.

The score is a predicted removal error. For a token-expert pair, the removal cost is tied to the squared router weight and the expert output energy ||E_u(z_t)||^2. The difficulty is that the true expert output is unavailable before the expert is fetched and executed, while selection must happen beforehand. BASE addresses this by training a lightweight linear predictor for each expert during calibration. At inference time, it predicts the expert’s output energy from the current token representation, combines that with router weights, aggregates the resulting costs across the batch, and selects the experts with the largest predicted batch-level impact.

The paper also handles the practical case where a token routes to an expert that was not loaded. It uses a backfill mechanism, replacing the missing expert with an available routed alternative. Compared with methods such as SERE and OEA, which build the batch active set more directly from token routing decisions, BASE asks a stronger question: how much does this expert matter to the current batch output? Compared with ExFold, which relies on calibrated expert norms, BASE uses token-conditioned predictions rather than static expert strength estimates.4c:T44f,The evaluation spans three MoE architectures and eight benchmarks, with comparisons under different batch budgets. The headline results reported in the paper are strong in the tight-budget regime: BASE improves average accuracy by 3.0 to 29.5 points over prior batch-aware decoding methods at comparable speed. Under more relaxed budgets, it stays within 0.4 points of dense or full-MoE quality while delivering 22% to 60% higher throughput.

The most important experimental checks are likely the ablations behind the method assumptions. One is the effect of dropping cross terms in the removal-error objective; the paper argues this has little impact on the selected expert set. Another is the quality of the output-energy predictor. If a simple linear model is sufficient, that suggests expert output energy is predictable enough from token representations to make the online procedure practical. Any plots showing how the batch-wise expert union grows with batch size, and how BASE controls that growth under a budget, are especially informative because they directly justify the problem formulation.4d:T45c,The main idea is a serving virtualization layer that separates the skipping policy from engine execution. A skipper exposes per-token RUN or Project-Only decisions at routed layers. vSkipper then realizes those decisions inside SGLang while preserving the engine’s batching and cache interfaces. RUN rows execute the layer normally. Project-Only rows bypass the layer’s attention and FFN, but still write the KV state needed by future autoregressive attention. This KV-complete treatment is the key correctness constraint: skipping hidden-state computation does not mean the layer can disappear from the cache. For execution, vSkipper packs rows with the same decision into cohorts at each routed layer, runs the corresponding computation, and scatters outputs back to the original batch positions. It also uses profitability-aware mode switching, routing only when estimated savings exceed the overhead of routing, packing, and dispatch. This differs from research implementations that route every step through specialized generation loops and often lose the saved compute to control-flow and batching overhead.4e:T7a3,SCSP changes the extraction pipeline rather than the model weights. The method has four components.

First, the document is partitioned into sentence-aware chunks, each capped at a maximum token length. This is not only for tractability. It narrows the semantic scope of the later compression prompt so that token-importance estimation happens in a more coherent local context.

Second, a short semantic-compression prompt such as “Brief summary: \"” is appended to each chunk. The prompt is not used to generate summaries explicitly. Instead, it is meant to trigger the model’s internal compression behavior, so that the prompt token’s attention pattern reflects which tokens in the chunk matter most semantically. The punctuation choice is deliberate: the colon and opening quote reduce the chance that the next-token distribution collapses onto punctuation continuation rather than semantic compression.

Third, the authors introduce a prompt-isolated attention mask. This mask prevents later document tokens from attending to the inserted prompts, which avoids contaminating the original document-token representations. At the same time, each prompt is restricted to attend only within its own chunk, so the resulting attention pattern is a local importance signal rather than a globally entangled one.

Fourth, token importance is estimated from the prompt-induced attention distributions, informative tokens are selected, and their representations from an intermediate layer are selectively pooled into the final embedding. Two design choices matter here. The method uses an intermediate layer rather than the final layer, consistent with the common observation that final layers in generative LLMs are often less suitable for semantic embedding geometry. And SCSP is designed as a plug-in on top of existing training-free methods such as Echo, TP, and HTP, so it complements prior work on backward information flow rather than replacing it.4f:T537,From the available full-text excerpt, the main empirical claim is that SCSP consistently improves several training-free long-context embedding baselines across multiple benchmarks, and can also further improve fine-tuned embedding models. The compared baselines include Echo, Token Prepending (TP), and Hierarchical Token Prepending (HTP). The gain is attributed to selective aggregation rather than another mechanism for fixing causal information flow.

The most important ablations are likely the following. First, sentence-aware chunking versus naive fixed-length chunking: if sentences are split arbitrarily, the compression prompt should produce noisier importance estimates. Second, the prompt-isolated mask: without isolation, the inserted prompts can interfere with document-token representations and reduce the benefit. Third, the token-selection ratio, the chosen extraction layer, and selective pooling versus mean pooling: these determine whether the method is truly benefiting from better token choice rather than from prompt insertion alone.

The provided excerpt does not include the full result tables or exact benchmark scores, so no specific numbers are claimed here. What is clear is the intended positioning: training-free, modular, and especially useful when long documents contain substantial semantic redundancy.50:T483,HeadGuard is a protection layer on top of an existing KV-cache quantizer, not a replacement quantization algorithm. Model weights stay in BF16. Text keys and values also stay in BF16. For image-token KV entries, unprotected heads are handled by the base quantizer, while selected image keys, or both keys and values, bypass quantization and remain in BF16. The selection is done offline. During calibration, two differentiable scalar gates are attached to each query head. The image gate scales the post-softmax attention weights on image-token columns without renormalization, measuring sensitivity of the correct-answer log probability to the image contribution. The output gate scales the whole head output and measures sensitivity through prompt-token next-token cross-entropy. The method uses mean absolute gradients as local first-order scores. For grouped-query attention, query-head scores are averaged into physical KV-head scores. Image-sensitivity and output-sensitivity scores are standardized, added, and the top-K physical KV heads are protected. The main experiments use roughly one eighth of all physical KV heads as the protection budget.51:T424,The evaluation covers eight VLMs, three base quantizers, and eight benchmarks. The models include LLaVA-1.5-7B, LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen2-VL-2B, Gemma-3-12B, Gemma-4-12B, Pixtral-12B, and InternVL3-8B. The discriminative tasks are POPE, MME, MMBench, image-based ScienceQA, multiple-choice MMMU, and SEED-Bench. TextVQA and COCO captioning are used for free-form generation.
